newsitem.title: FINLAND: FOCUS - UPM-Kymmene up despite profit fall.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - UPM-Kymmene up despite profit fall.

text.p: Europe's largest forestry group UPM-Kymmene Oy on Tuesday reported weak 1996 profits, but said it expected a steady performance this year.

With profit before extraordinary items down 43 percent to 3.56 billion markka ($698 million) from a record 6.28 billion in the bumper year 1995. UPM-Kymmene held the value of its dividend at 4.50 markka, much of it in stock in a subsidiary.
Its net 1996 sales fell to 51.75 billion markka from 54.74 billion, with operating profit down less sharply than profit after extras to 5.59 billion markka from 8.50 billion.
Although there was initial disappointment with the profit, which was below average forecasts of 3.7 billion markka, analysts saw healthy signs for the sector in the company's comments.
They said the market had anticipated worse news, and UPM's shares reversed early losses to rise more than three markka to 108 in early afternoon trade.
"The result was in line with what we expected and it was a good outlook," said Bjorn Danckwardt-Liljestrom, forest industry analyst at Swedish Handelsbanken.

Analysts also called UPM's decision to pay only 1.50 markka of its 4.50 dividend in cash and 3.00 markka in shares in engineering group Rauma Oy, in which UPM owns a stake of 73.3 percent, was a good move for the company.
"It saves them cash," said Arctos forestry analyst Jukka Huuskonen. "For UPM's shareholders, this is a good arrangement."
If the payout is approved, this would reduce UPM-Kymmene's stake in Rauma to 59.9 percent, the company said.
"In the future it is intended to reduce this to below 50 percent through other means," it said.
Rauma, reporting simultaneously with its parent company, said its profit nudged up to 679 million markka from 671 million in 1995 and it too forecast a steady 1996 showing.
UPM said in a statement it expected this year's profit to be similar to last year and chief executive Juha Niemela told Reuters Financial Television that there was a chance for improvement.
"There are possibilities for better results, but we cannot rely on that development yet," Niemela said.

UPM's operating results in 1996 were hardest hit in chemical pulp, which plunged into a 176 million markka loss from a 2.23 billion profit in 1995. Pulp prices fell very sharply last year following a build-up of stocks.
Fine papers, too, only made a modest 85 million markka profit, down from 719 million.
Analysts said developments early this year showed the level of overall forest sector stocks had normalised.
"Now it is all about how actual demand develops and ... it revolves pretty much around how the German economy develops," said AG Private Bankers chief analyst Jussi Hyoty.
UPM said economic growth was expected to increase gradually in Europe, the company's main market, and this would increase paper consumption.

"Deliveries of printing and writing papers are expected to be up on 1996, although sales prices will be lower, at least in the early part of the year," it said. Printing paper prices have probably bottomed out, it added.
Analysts expected average prices this year would be below last year's but said volumes would be higher. UPM said it hoped to raise fine paper and LWC prices during the first quarter.
Niemela told a news conference UPM would try to raise fine paper prises by 10 percent, but the outcome was uncertain.
He expected pulp prices, which are sensitive to the forest industry outlook, to continue falling at a rate of about $1 to $2 per month in the near term ($ = 5.097 Finnish Markka)
